key_insight: In psychiatric diagnosis, two LLMs can look equally accurate but still differ meaningfully in the quality of their reasoning, so accuracy alone can miss important model differences.
clinical_relevance: For clinical AI evaluation, this suggests clinicians should assess not just whether a model gets the right diagnosis, but how well its reasoning supports safe and trustworthy use.
method: 4 frontier LLMs generated ranked top-5 psychiatric differentials for 196 vignettes.
An automated adjudicator scored diagnostic accuracy across cases and generation runs.
Five blinded psychiatrists rated correctness and reasoning on 30 vignettes using a 0–4 rubric.
evidence_signal: On the 30 clinician-rated vignettes, accuracy separated no model pair, but reasoning separated five pairs; one equally accurate pair differed by 0.70 reasoning points.
watch_item: Automated accuracy depended on adjudication details and was less aligned with clinician judgment than clinician-to-clinician agreement, so implementation should not rely on accuracy-only benchmarking.
paper_title: Diagnostic accuracy and clinician-rated reasoning quality dissociate in a blinded evaluation of large language models in psychiatry
